query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, the initially homogeneous (metastable) solid solution partially decomposes during post-processing (e.g., a controlled heat treatment) into fine intermetallic phases. These phases, owing to differences in elemental affinities and diffusion kinetics, promote the localized formation of passivating oxide layers (e.g., enriched in Ti/Zn oxides) that lower corrosion current densities and improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy exhibiting a primarily metastable single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-casting heat treatment designed to trigger phase separation and the formation of fine intermetallic compounds.
generation.conditions: Testing performed under conditions maintaining a density below 6 g/cm³; heat treatment at an elevated temperature (yet below the melting point) under inert atmosphere followed by environmental exposure for corrosion and high-temperature oxidation tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of fine-scale intermetallic phases (e.g., Mg-rich and Ti/Zn-rich compounds) that mediate the nucleation and stabilization of passivating oxide films.
generation.mechanism: Differences in constituent element properties (e.g., diffusion rates and oxide-forming tendencies) drive phase separation from the metastable solid solution during heat treatment. The resulting intermetallic domains then serve as preferential nucleation sites for protective oxide films. These films modify the local chemistry at the alloy surface, thereby reducing corrosive attack and slowing high-temperature oxide growth.
generation.predicted_outcome: After heat treatment, the alloy will show a measurable increase in the fraction of intermetallic phases along with a decreased corrosion current density and enhanced stability (e.g., lower oxide growth rate) at high temperature when compared to the as-cast baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-cast alloy exhibiting a metastable single-phase solid solution with standard corrosion and oxidation behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to lightweight high-entropy alloy compositions engineered to remain below 6 g/cm³ and processed under non-equilibrium conditions (e.g., induction melting and rapid consolidation methods such as ball milling and spark plasma sintering).
generation.uncertainty: The exact phase fractions, intermetallic sizes, and kinetic parameters of phase evolution are not precisely known, and the balance between beneficial passivation and any possible detrimental galvanic effects from heterogeneous intermetallic distribution remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same as-cast Mg-containing high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to a controlled heat treatment intended to induce phase separation, while leaving the other as-cast. Perform microstructural analysis (via SEM, EDS, and XRD) to quantify and compare the formation of intermetallic phases. Then, conduct standardized corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests (monitoring mass gain and oxide composition by XRD and XPS) on both sets.
measurements: Quantification of intermetallic phase fractions and distribution
Corrosion potential and corrosion current density measurements
Oxidation kinetics (mass change over time) and oxide film composition analyses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in intermetallic phase formation and do not demonstrate improved corrosion resistance or slower oxidation kinetics compared to the as-cast baseline, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), which include multiple principal elements, have attracted substantial research attention due to their exceptional mechanical properties, such as high fracture toughness, hardness, fatigue and corrosion resistances, yield strength, ductility and thermal stability,,,. In many applications, HEAs can significantly outperform traditional and super-alloys, especially at low and high temperatures,. Recently, the design of lightweight HEAs (with a density lower than 5 g/cc) has become one of the hottest research topics in metallurgy. In view of the outstanding performance of HEAs, the lightweight HEAs may have superior performance than traditional lightweight materials such as Al, Mg, and Ti alloys, with a large number of potential industry applications. Yet the chemical and compositional design space of HEAs is exceptionally vast, which makes the use of the traditional experimental methods for HEA screening an overwhelming task. Thus, an efficient, accurate strategy is required for the design of lightweight HEAs for specific applications,. The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.
